title: Stars, Faith, and a Covenant Cut in the Dark
summary: God tells a childless Abram that he will have a son of his own and descendants as many as the stars, and Abram believes him. When Abram asks how he can know he will possess the land, God has him cut animals in half, foretells four centuries of slavery and a return, and then passes alone between the pieces as a smoking firepot and a flaming torch, binding himself by covenant.
story:
In Genesis 12 God promised Abram land, a great nation, and blessing for every family on earth. Years have passed. Abram has just rescued Lot from four invading kings, been blessed by Melchizedek, and refused the king of Sodom's offer of the plunder (Genesis 14), yet he still has no child. The promise of a nation hangs on a son who doesn't exist, and the only heir in view is a servant.

This chapter is where the promise becomes a covenant, a solemn and binding commitment sealed by a ritual, and where Abram's response is named for the first time as faith. It also looks far ahead, past Abram's own peaceful death, through slavery in a foreign land, to the exodus and the return to Canaan. The next chapter shows Abram and Sarai trying to secure the promised son by their own means through Hagar, and chapter 17 adds the sign of circumcision and names Sarah as the mother of the promised child. Genesis 15 stands between the call and those later events as the chapter where God swears.
historical:
The patriarchs are traditionally placed in the early second millennium BC, and those who read Genesis's chronology as history set Abram there; many scholars doubt the patriarchal stories can be dated at all, or see them as traditions shaped much later (see the note on Genesis 12 and the introduction). The childless man whose servant would inherit has been compared with tablets from Nuzi in northern Mesopotamia (fifteenth and fourteenth centuries BC), where childless couples sometimes adopted an heir, sometimes a servant, with the arrangement changing if a natural son was later born. Mid-twentieth-century scholars leaned hard on such parallels; Thomas L. Thompson (The Historicity of the Patriarchal Narratives, 1974) and John Van Seters (Abraham in History and Tradition, 1975) showed that many were overstated and that similar customs span a long period and many places. The broad point stands: a household without a son needed a legal heir, and Abram has only Eliezer, a servant from Damascus, one of the oldest cities of Syria and later the capital of the Aramean kingdom that fought Israel.

The peoples named in verses 19 to 21 belong to the old population of Canaan. The Amorites of verse 16 bear a name from the Akkadian Amurru, ‘the west’, used in Mesopotamian texts of the late third and early second millennium for western Semitic peoples; Amorite dynasties ruled much of Mesopotamia in that age, including the dynasty of Hammurabi of Babylon (eighteenth century BC). In the Bible the name often stands for the inhabitants of Canaan in general (Amos 2:9-10). The Rephaim appear in Genesis 14:5 and Deuteronomy 2:11 as an ancient people of great stature; texts from Ugarit use the related word rpum for the honored dead, which is why the Hebrew word can also mean shades of the dead (Isaiah 14:9). The Hittites of Genesis are local ‘sons of Heth’ (Genesis 23) rather than the empire of Anatolia, though scholars debate how the two relate. The borders of verse 18, from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates, were approached only under David and Solomon (1 Kings 4:21).

The four hundred years of verse 13 point forward to the sojourn in Egypt and the exodus. The date of the exodus is contested. First Kings 6:1 counts 480 years from the exodus to the fourth year of Solomon, which gives a date around 1446 BC; many scholars prefer the thirteenth century, when Egyptian kings of the Nineteenth Dynasty built the city of Pi-Ramesses in the eastern Nile delta, since Exodus 1:11 names the store city Rameses. Ancient readers already counted the four hundred years differently: the Hebrew of Exodus 12:40 gives 430 years for the stay in Egypt, the Septuagint and Samaritan Pentateuch count the 430 years for Canaan and Egypt together, Paul counts 430 years from the promise to the law (Galatians 3:17), and rabbinic chronology (followed by Rashi on Exodus 12:40) counted 400 years from Isaac's birth and 430 from this covenant, leaving about 210 years in Egypt.
cultural:
Two images open the chapter. God calls himself Abram's shield (magen), a word used of kings as protectors of their people (Psalm 84:9, 89:18), and a pointed one after chapter 14, where Melchizedek blessed the God who ‘delivered’ (miggen, from the same root) Abram's enemies into his hand. He also promises a reward (sakhar), the ordinary word for a soldier's or worker's wages; Abram had just refused the king of Sodom's plunder (14:22-23), and God now offers himself, or a very great reward, in its place.

The ritual in verses 9 to 17 was a known way of making a binding agreement. Hebrew speaks of ‘cutting’ a covenant (karat berit), and here the phrase is literal. At Mari on the Euphrates (eighteenth century BC), letters speak of concluding a treaty by ‘killing a donkey foal’, and one letter reports that a puppy and a goat were rejected as unfit for the rite. In the treaty of the Assyrian king Ashur-nirari V with Mati'ilu of Arpad (about 754 BC), a lamb's head is cut off with the words that it is not the head of a lamb but the head of Mati'ilu, his sons, and his people, should he break the treaty. The Aramaic treaty from Sefire in Syria (eighth century BC) contains a similar curse, that as a calf is cut in two, so the vassal and his nobles will be cut in two. Jeremiah 34:18 describes Judah's leaders making a covenant during the Babylonian siege (about 588 BC) by cutting a calf in two and walking between its parts, and God says he will treat covenant-breakers “like the calf they cut in two in order to pass between its pieces.” The meaning is a self-curse: may what happened to these animals happen to me if I break my word.

What would have startled an ancient reader is who walks the path. Normally the party taking the oath, usually the weaker party, passes between the pieces. Here Abram doesn't walk at all. Birds of prey come down and he drives them off; then, as the sun sets, he falls into a deep sleep, the tardemah God sent on the man in 2:21, and is overwhelmed by great terror and darkness. After dark a smoking firepot (tannur, a clay oven or brazier) and a flaming torch pass through alone. Fire and smoke are signs of God's presence throughout the Old Testament: the burning bush (Exodus 3:2), the pillar of cloud and fire (Exodus 13:21), and the smoke on Sinai (Exodus 19:18). God binds himself. The animals Abram brings, a heifer, a goat, a ram, a turtledove, and a young pigeon, are all animals Israel's law later accepts for sacrifice, and the birds are left whole as the law later requires for a bird offering (Leviticus 1:17).

The promise of verse 15, that Abram will ‘go to his fathers in peace’ and be buried at a good old age, expresses the ancient hope for a death that is full, peaceful, and followed by honorable burial, which Genesis records in 25:8. The fourth generation of verse 16 uses dor, which can mean a single step in a family tree or a lifetime or era; Exodus 6:16-20 counts four generations from Levi to Moses.
literary:
The chapter has two matching halves, each opening with God's self-introduction and Abram's question. In verses 1 to 6 God is Abram's shield and reward; Abram asks what God can give a childless man; God answers with the stars; Abram believes. In verses 7 to 21 God is the one who brought Abram from Ur; Abram asks, “how can I know that I will possess it?”; God answers with a covenant ritual. The first half turns on seeing the night sky, the second on sunset, deep sleep, terror, and darkness. The first half is about a son, the second about land. Verse 6, a single sentence of the narrator's comment set outside the dialogue, sits at the hinge.

The chapter is full of firsts. It is the first time Scripture says ‘the word of the LORD came’ to someone, the formula of the prophets (Jeremiah 1:2), and the first time God says ‘Do not be afraid’. It contains the first use of the verb believe and the first time Abram speaks to God at length, and his first words are a complaint. Genesis 20:7 will call Abraham a prophet, and this chapter reads like a prophetic call and vision: a word that comes, a vision by night, a deep sleep, and an oracle about the distant future.

The self-introduction of verse 7, “I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans”, uses the same words that open the Ten Commandments, ‘I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt’ (Exodus 20:2), so Abram's departure is presented as a first exodus. The oracle of verses 13 to 16 then summarizes the whole book of Exodus in four sentences: sojourn, slavery, affliction, judgment on the oppressor, departure with possessions, and return. The key verbs repeat from half to half, especially know (yada, verses 8 and 13) and possess or inherit (yarash, verses 3, 4, 7, 8). The chapter closes not with Abram's response but with a list of ten peoples, the longest such list in the Bible, which makes the reader feel both the size of the gift and the length of the wait.

outline.t: A son and descendants like the stars; Abram believes
Abram asks for assurance and prepares the animals
In deep darkness, God foretells slavery and return
God passes between the pieces and makes a covenant

doctrines.note: “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (verse 6). Righteousness is counted to Abram on the basis of trust in God's promise, before circumcision (Genesis 17) and before the law. Paul builds his teaching on justification by faith directly on this verse (Romans 4:3-11, Galatians 3:6-9), and James cites it to show that such faith is proved in action (James 2:23). Christians differ on how reckoning and renewal relate, but all read the verse as putting God's promise and Abram's trust first.

Abram is old and his wife barren, yet he believes (verse 6). The verb means to rest one's weight on someone as reliable. Faith here is reliance on the one who made the promise, not confidence in circumstances, and it coexists with honest questions: Abram complains before he believes (verses 2 and 3) and asks for assurance after (verse 8), and God answers both without rebuke.

God alone passes between the pieces (verse 17), taking on himself the curse that such rituals invoked. The land promise rests on God's commitment rather than Abram's performance. Later covenants add obligations, but this one shows the foundation: a God who binds himself by oath, which Hebrews 6:13-18 calls the anchor of Christian hope.

God tells Abram of four centuries of slavery before they happen (verse 13). The oppression of Exodus 1 is therefore not the failure of the promise but part of a history God foresaw, set limits to, and would bring to its end, including his judgment on the oppressing nation (verse 14).

The land will not be given until ‘the iniquity of the Amorites’ is complete (verse 16). The later conquest is framed as judgment on accumulated wrongdoing after long patience, not as favoritism, and Leviticus 18:24-28 holds Israel to the same standard: the land that expelled the Canaanites for these practices will expel Israel too.

words.note: Aman, to be firm or reliable; in the causative (Hiphil) form used here, to believe or trust, literally to regard as firm. The root occurs about a hundred times and gives Hebrew amen (‘surely’) and emunah (‘faithfulness’). With the preposition be, as here, it means to put trust in someone. Verse 6 is its first appearance as ‘believe’ in the Bible. Habakkuk 2:4 uses the noun emunah in the line Paul quotes beside this verse (Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11). Standard lexicons (BDB, HALOT) distinguish the Hiphil sense, to trust, from the passive sense, to be faithful, and interpreters debate how far the two overlap here.

Chashav, to think, plan, reckon, or count (about 120 occurrences). It includes the bookkeeping sense of crediting something to an account, and is used when an offering is or is not ‘credited’ to the worshiper (Leviticus 7:18) and when Phinehas's zeal is ‘credited to him as righteousness’ (Psalm 106:31). Gerhard von Rad (Theologische Literaturzeitung, 1951) argued that the verb echoes the priestly declaration that a sacrifice was accepted, applied here to faith instead of a sacrifice. The subject of the verb is disputed: most take it to be God; a minority of medieval Jewish interpreters, including Nachmanides, read Abram as the one who reckoned God's promise as righteousness on God's part.

Tsedaqah, righteousness (about 160 occurrences, especially in Isaiah and the Psalms). In Hebrew it is a relational word: being in the right, doing what a relationship requires, and so right standing before a judge or loyalty to a covenant. Later Hebrew uses it for charity. In verse 6 Abram is not called morally perfect (chapters 12, 16, and 20 show otherwise); he is counted as being in the right with God. Genesis 18:19 uses the same word for what Abraham's household must practice, literally doing ‘righteousness and justice’ (the BSB's “what is right and just”).

Berit, covenant (about 285 occurrences): a formal, binding bond between parties, sealed with oaths, rituals, and signs. It can be between equals, between a king and a vassal, or between God and people. The Bible's story is carried by a series of covenants, with Noah (Genesis 9), Abraham (here and chapter 17), Israel at Sinai, David (2 Samuel 7, called a covenant in Psalm 89), and the new covenant Jeremiah promised (Jeremiah 31:31). This is the first covenant God makes with Abram, and its only sworn party is God.

Karat, to cut, cut off, or cut down (nearly 290 occurrences). With berit it forms the standard idiom for making a covenant, ‘to cut a covenant’, which recalls rituals like this one. The same verb is used for being ‘cut off’ from the people as a covenant penalty (Genesis 17:14). In this chapter the idiom appears in verse 18 after the ritual has been performed, so the reader sees the cutting before hearing the phrase.

Magen, shield (about 60 occurrences, a third of them in the Psalms). It is the small round shield of an infantryman, and it becomes a title for God as protector (Psalm 3:3, 18:2, 84:11) and for kings as protectors of their people (Psalm 84:9, 89:18). In verse 1 God says ‘I am your shield’ to a man who has just made enemies of four eastern kings, and the word plays on miggen, ‘delivered’, in Melchizedek's blessing (14:20).

Yarash, to take possession, inherit, or dispossess (about 230 occurrences, seventy of them in Deuteronomy). The verb joins the chapter's two halves: in verses 3 and 4 the question is who will inherit Abram's household, and in verses 7 and 8 it is whether Abram will possess the land. In the conquest books it describes Israel taking the land and the nations being driven out, and in the Psalms it becomes the hope that the meek will inherit the land (Psalm 37:11), which Jesus takes up in Matthew 5:5.

christ:
Genesis 15:6 is among the Old Testament verses the New Testament uses most. Paul quotes it in Romans 4 and Galatians 3 to argue that God counts people righteous through faith, not works of the law. His argument turns on timing: “Was it after his circumcision, or before? It was not after, but before” (Romans 4:10), so that Abraham is “the father of all who believe but are not circumcised” (Romans 4:11) as well as of the circumcised who share his faith. He ends by applying the verse to Christian faith: the words were written “not only for Abraham, but also for us, to whom righteousness will be credited—for us who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead” (Romans 4:23-24). Abram trusted a God who could bring life from a body as good as dead; Christians trust the God who raised Jesus. James 2:21-23 cites the same verse to insist that real faith shows itself in obedience, and says it was ‘fulfilled’ when Abraham offered Isaac.

Hebrews 6:13-20 points to God swearing by himself to Abraham (the oath of Genesis 22:16-17, which carries forward the self-binding pictured here) as an anchor for Christian hope, since “it is impossible for God to lie” (Hebrews 6:18). Hebrews 11:12 recalls the stars of verse 5. In Galatians 3:17 Paul counts the 430 years of Exodus 12:40 from the promise to the law, and argues that the law cannot annul a covenant God had already ratified; the promise, sealed here, stands underneath everything that follows. Zechariah's song rejoices that God has remembered “the oath He swore to our father Abraham” (Luke 1:73), and Mary's song ends with the same promise (Luke 1:55).

The oracle of verses 13 to 16 anticipates the exodus, and the New Testament uses the exodus to describe the work of Christ: Luke 9:31 calls Jesus' coming death his ‘departure’, literally his exodos, and Paul calls Christ ‘our Passover lamb’ (1 Corinthians 5:7). Many Christians also see in God's walking alone between the pieces a picture of grace that takes the curse on itself, and connect it with the cross, where Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). Meredith Kline (By Oath Consigned, 1968) developed this reading of the ritual as a self-curse. That is a theological reading of the pattern, not a link the New Testament draws from this passage, and it should be taught as such.
interpretation:
Jewish readers of the Second Temple period read this chapter closely. Jubilees 14 retells it and dates the covenant between the pieces to the middle of the third month, the season of the feast of weeks, which Jubilees treats as the festival of covenant renewal. The Apocalypse of Abraham (first or second century AD) expands verses 9 to 17 into a heavenly vision in which an angel named Yahoel guides Abram's sacrifice and the fallen angel Azazel comes down like the birds of prey. Philo's Who Is the Heir of Divine Things? is an allegorical commentary on verses 2 to 18. The chapter's key verse was already read in two directions. First Maccabees 2:52 asks whether Abraham was not ‘found faithful when tested’ and so reckoned righteous, joining Genesis 15:6 to the binding of Isaac, and the Qumran letter 4QMMT speaks of deeds being reckoned as righteousness.

The rabbis called the rite the covenant between the pieces (berit bein ha-betarim). Genesis Rabbah 44 reads the animals and the ‘terror’ and ‘great darkness’ of verse 12 as the four kingdoms that would oppress Israel, Babylon, Media, Greece, and Rome (44:17). Rashi read verse 6 as God counting Abram's faith to him as merit (tsedaqah); Nachmanides objected that believing God's promise hardly needed to be counted as merit and proposed that Abram counted the promise as God's righteousness. Rashi (on Exodus 12:40) followed the rabbinic chronology that counted the 430 years from this covenant.

Christian reading began with Paul, Hebrews, and James. Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 23, around 160) argued that Abraham was justified by faith while uncircumcised and received circumcision as a sign. The verse became central in the Reformation: Luther's Lectures on Genesis (1535-1545) and Calvin's commentary (1554) read it as the Old Testament's clearest statement of righteousness reckoned to faith, while the Council of Trent's Decree on Justification (1547) taught that justification includes inner renewal and that faith is its beginning. Modern scholarship has added von Rad's 1951 essay on the priestly background of ‘reckoning’; the debate over the rite between Gerhard Hasel (Journal for the Study of the Old Testament 19, 1981), who read it against treaty rituals, and Gordon Wenham (JSOT 22, 1982), who read the animals as symbols of Israel and the birds of prey as the nations; and, in New Testament studies, E. P. Sanders's Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977) and N. T. Wright's Paul and the Faithfulness of God (2013), which read Romans 4 as an argument about who belongs to Abraham's family as much as about how an individual is justified.

In the synagogue the chapter belongs to the portion Lekh Lekha (Genesis 12:1-17:27). The Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 1 to 12 and 17 to 18 on the Second Sunday in Lent in Year C, and verses 1 to 6 at Proper 14 in Year C beside Hebrews 11, which celebrates the faith of those who, like Abram, ‘saw’ the promises only from afar.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter.

In verse 1 the Hebrew can mean that God is Abram's reward or that Abram's reward will be very great. The King James Version (‘thy exceeding great reward’), the NIV, and the BSB take the first; the ESV and NRSV take the second (‘your reward shall be very great’), as does the Septuagint. In verse 2 the phrase ben-mesheq beiti, rendered ‘the heir of my house’ or ‘the steward of my house’ (KJV), uses a word found only here that seems to play on Dammeseq, Damascus; its exact meaning is uncertain.

Verse 6 has an important difference between the Hebrew and the Greek. The Hebrew says ‘he (God) reckoned it to him as righteousness’, with an active verb. The Septuagint reads ‘Abram believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness’, with a passive verb and ‘God’ rather than the divine name. Paul and James quote the Greek form, which is why the New Testament reads “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Romans 4:3), and many English versions, including the BSB, use the passive in Genesis as well. The ESV and NIV keep the active (‘he counted it’, ‘he credited it’).

In verse 13 the four hundred years stand beside 430 years in Exodus 12:40; there the Septuagint and Samaritan Pentateuch add ‘and in the land of Canaan’, counting the patriarchs' time in Canaan within the 430, which shortens the stay in Egypt (see the historical note). In verse 17 the King James Version's ‘a smoking furnace, and a burning lamp’ renders the same Hebrew as modern versions' ‘smoking firepot’ and ‘flaming torch’. In verse 18 the perfect verb natatti is rendered ‘I have given’ (KJV, BSB) or ‘I give’ (ESV, NIV); it presents the gift as already done. The Hebrew and English verse numbers are the same throughout.

teach.big: When the promise seems impossible, God answers honest doubt by showing Abram the stars and binding himself by covenant, and Abram's trust in that promise is counted as righteousness.

outline.t: God meets fear with himself (‘I am your shield, your very great reward’), and Abram answers with an honest complaint about the one thing he lacks. Lament is not unbelief.
God answers the complaint with a sharper promise and a sign in the sky, and Abram believes. Righteousness is credited to trust in God's word, before any law or ritual.
Faith can still ask ‘how can I know?’ God answers not with rebuke but with a covenant ceremony, and Abram waits through the day, guarding the pieces.
The promise includes darkness: four centuries of slavery lie ahead. God's timing takes account of his justice toward other nations and his care for Abram's descendants.
God alone passes between the pieces. The covenant rests on God's self-commitment, and the land is described as already given.

teach.pitfalls:
The most common misuse of verse 6 turns faith into a work of its own, a mental effort that earns God's approval. The text credits righteousness to Abram's trust, but the weight falls on the one trusted: Abram believed the LORD. A second misuse sets Paul and James against each other. Both quote the same verse; Paul uses it to show that righteousness is not earned by works of the law, James to show that genuine faith is not idle. Teach them together.

A third pitfall treats Abram's question in verse 8 as unbelief to be condemned. God answers it with a covenant, which suggests the question was the right one to ask. A fourth makes the animals an allegory, each standing for a particular doctrine or nation; Genesis Rabbah and Wenham offered symbolic readings, but the text itself explains the ritual only through Jeremiah 34 and leaves the rest unstated. Finally, do not skip verses 13 to 16 as a detour. The promise of slavery and the patience toward the Amorites are part of the gospel of this chapter: God's promises do not exempt his people from suffering, and his justice is not favoritism.
teach.pastoral: This chapter speaks to people waiting for what they long for, especially the childless. Abram's complaint in verses 2 and 3 is voiced without shame, and God does not rebuke it; teachers can let the room know that grief and honest questions are welcome in prayer. Be careful not to turn the stars into a promise that everyone who believes will receive a child or whatever they are waiting for; Abram's promise was particular, and Hebrews 11:13 says many died in faith without receiving what was promised. The chapter also speaks to those whose faith feels unsteady. Abram believes and then asks for assurance, and God responds by binding himself. Those troubled by scrupulosity, who fear that their faith is never strong enough, can be pointed to the one who walks between the pieces: the covenant's certainty rests on God, not on the strength of the believer's grip.

hard.q: Does Genesis 15:6 really teach that God counts faith as righteousness apart from works, as Paul says?
hard.a:
The objection is ancient and serious. Many Jewish readers have taken the verse to commend Abram's faithfulness as a merit God rewards. First Maccabees 2:52 links the verse to Abraham being ‘found faithful when tested’, that is, to his obedience in Genesis 22, and Rashi explains that God counted Abram's faith to him as merit. Nachmanides proposed a different reading in which Abram, not God, is the subject: Abram counted God's promise as an act of God's righteousness. James 2:21-24 appears to read the verse with works in view, saying that Abraham was justified by what he did when he offered Isaac and that the Scripture was then ‘fulfilled’. Critics of the Reformation reading, from the Council of Trent (1547) to many modern scholars, argue that Paul's contrast between faith and works has been read back into a verse that does not make it, and E. P. Sanders (Paul and Palestinian Judaism, 1977) argued that the Judaism of Paul's day was not a religion of earning salvation by works in the first place.

The responses come from different traditions. Paul's own argument rests on what the text says and when: Abram is counted righteous in chapter 15, years before circumcision in chapter 17 and centuries before the law (Romans 4:10, Galatians 3:17), and the verse speaks of believing, not doing. Gerhard von Rad (1951) argued that the verb echoes the priest's declaration that a sacrifice was accepted, and that Genesis here transfers that declaration from a ritual act to faith, a reading that supports Paul's emphasis. Luther and Calvin read ‘credited’ as God reckoning to the believer a righteousness not his own. Roman Catholic and Orthodox theology, as at Trent, holds that the God who reckons righteous also makes righteous, so that faith, the beginning of justification, is not separated from renewal and works of love. Many interpreters harmonize Paul and James by noting that Paul speaks of how Abraham was first counted righteous and James of how that faith was shown and ‘completed’ in Genesis 22. N. T. Wright (Paul and the Faithfulness of God, 2013) and others in the ‘New Perspective’ read Paul's use of the verse as chiefly about who belongs to Abraham's family, Gentiles included, without the works of the law that marked Jewish identity. Christians continue to differ on how reckoning and renewal relate; all agree that the verse puts God's promise and Abram's trust before any merit of his own.

hard.q: Why must the land wait because “the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete”, and how does that fit with the later conquest?
hard.a:
The objection is moral and historical. Verse 16 looks ahead to Israel's conquest of Canaan, which Deuteronomy and Joshua describe in terms of total destruction. Thomas Paine (The Age of Reason, 1794-1807) attacked the Old Testament's war narratives as incompatible with a good God, and many modern readers share that judgment. Eric Seibert (Disturbing Divine Behavior, 2009), writing as a Christian scholar, argues that the portrait of God commanding the destruction of peoples reflects Israel's own views rather than God's character as revealed in Jesus, and that readers should distinguish the textual God from the actual God. The chronology adds a lesser difficulty: four hundred years in verse 13, the fourth generation in verse 16, and 430 years in Exodus 12:40.

Defenders of the text begin with what this verse says. It frames the later conquest as judgment on long-standing wrongdoing, not ethnic favoritism, and it shows God waiting four centuries rather than acting at once. Deuteronomy 9:4-5 insists that Israel receives the land “because of their wickedness” and not because of Israel's own righteousness, and Leviticus 18:24-28 warns that the land will vomit out Israel too if it does the same things, which is what the exile later showed. Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan (Did God Really Command Genocide?, 2014) argue that the language of total destruction is ancient war rhetoric, hyperbole of a kind found in other Near Eastern annals, and that Joshua and Judges themselves assume many Canaanites remained. Christopher J. H. Wright (The God I Don't Understand, 2008) accepts that the texts remain painful and holds that the conquest was a unique act of judgment, not a pattern for any later people. Seibert's approach is rejected by many as setting Scripture against itself, while others value it for taking the moral question seriously. On the numbers, many take four hundred as a round figure for the 430 years and read ‘generation’ in verse 16 as a lifetime or era; the four generations from Levi to Moses (Exodus 6:16-20) fit the verse. Readers still differ on how literally to take the conquest accounts, but this verse presents a God patient with nations outside his covenant who holds his own people to the same standard.

observe: How does God describe himself in verse 1 and again in verse 7? What question does Abram ask after each self-description?
What does Abram do between verse 10 and verse 17, and who passes between the pieces?
List what God tells Abram about the future in verses 13 to 16. Which parts are hard news and which are good news?
interpret: Verse 6 comes right after Abram has complained and just before he asks for assurance. What does its placement suggest about the nature of faith?
In light of Jeremiah 34:18, what did it mean for God alone to pass between the pieces?
Why might God tell Abram about four centuries of slavery at the very moment he makes the covenant?
apply: Abram believed God when nothing in his circumstances supported the promise. What makes it hard for you to trust a promise you cannot yet see fulfilled?
Abram brought his complaint and his question to God, and God answered both. What honest question or lament do you need to bring to God rather than hide?
How does it change your view of God to see him bind himself to his promises rather than wait for you to earn them?
